native_result.query: In what scenario did urban land use promote a specific type of plant invasion?
native_result.HypoA: Urban land use reduced invasion by gardening plants over unintentionally introduced ones.
native_result.HypoB: Urban land use promoted a specific type of plant invasion in the scenario of consolidated, spatially extensive urbanization (the 'Urban' habitat and high urban cover persisting since before 1956, best detected at the 500 m neighbourhood buffer, strengthening through 1993–2009). Under this scenario, invasions are dominated by UNINTENTIONALLY introduced annual ruderal herbs of low stature and broad invaded niche — mainly Asteraceae and Amaranthaceae (Erigeron/Conyza spp., Amaranthus retroflexus, Symphyotrichum squamatum, Xanthium spp.) — rather than by ornamental garden escapes, which are predominantly perennial/woody (Robinia pseudoacacia, Pittosporum tobira, Lonicera japonica). New progressive urban/cropland expansion does not (yet) host these unintentional invaders; the effect belongs to long-established urban landscapes. The pathway-specific invasion types are phylogenetically structured (adjacent tree tips share pathway more than expected by chance, p=0.008).
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Verified inputs (temporal 12×3 contingency; species traits 81×19 with 77 unique species and 4 dual-pathway duplicates; plot data 632×37 with 0 NAs; Newick tree 79 tips matching 79/81 phylo.tip.label). 2) Habitat × pathway composition of 632 plots: chi-square tests (10-habitat χ²=75.2, p=5.8e-9; Urban vs rest χ²=10.1, p=0.0064) plus Poisson GLMs with HC0 robust SEs (Urban IRR: unintentional 4.9, gardening 3.2; adjusted for elevation/climate: 2.5 and 1.68). 3) Buffer/epoch consistency scan without prior selection: Spearman correlations of urban cover (50/500/1000 m × 1956/1993/2009) and progressive trajectories vs per-plot pathway counts — 500 m buffer and 2009 strongest (ρ(n.total)=0.55), progressive 1956–2009 negatively associated with unintentional counts (ρ=−0.13); trajectory-group contrasts (Kruskal n.unint H=21.0, p=3e-5) and 'established urban' plots comparison (2.05 vs 0.61 invaders/plot, Mann-Whitney p<1e-4). 4) Species traits by pathway: chi-square (growth.form p=3.2e-6; dispersal p=0.43; vegetative p=0.22) and Kruskal-Wallis (height p=1.2e-5; invaded niche breadth p=0.047; mrt p=0.28; invasion extent p=0.083). 5) Temporal trends: pathway composition across 4 introduction periods (χ²=230.4, p<1e-46; Gardening introductions rise to 75% in 1985–2019). 6) Phylogenetic support: permutation test of pathway clustering along the Newick tree tip order (adjacent same-pathway 55.1% vs 41.7% null, p=0.008, 9999 permutations; Opuntia ficus-indica entries excluded from phylo, kept for pathway analyses). 7) Non-unit sums of progressive+regressive+no.changes documented (125/632 and 124/632 rows, range 0–1.01) and left unrenormalized (marginal impact).

gold_sub_hypo.full_hypo: Urban land use reduced invasion by gardening plants over unintentionally introduced ones.

sub_hypo.text: Consolidated, spatially extensive urbanization promotes plant invasion, especially through unintentional introduction rather than gardening.
sub_hypo.context: Sampled plots in Barcelona province, specifically the Urban habitat and landscapes with high urban cover persisting since before 1956; the association is best detected within 500 m and strengthens through 1993–2009.
sub_hypo.relations: Established urban landscapes have higher invasion counts (2.05 versus 0.61 invaders per plot). Urban habitat has a stronger positive association with unintentional counts than gardening counts (IRRs 4.9 versus 3.2; elevation/climate-adjusted IRRs 2.5 versus 1.68). Urban cover at 500 m in 2009 has the strongest association with total counts (Spearman ρ=0.55).

sub_hypo.text: The unintentional invaders characteristic of established urban landscapes are low-stature annual ruderal herbs with broad invaded niches, whereas ornamental garden escapes are predominantly perennial or woody.
sub_hypo.context: Non-native plants in Barcelona province, interpreted within the established urban invasion scenario. Unintentional examples are mainly Asteraceae and Amaranthaceae: Erigeron/Conyza spp., Amaranthus retroflexus, Symphyotrichum squamatum and Xanthium spp. Gardening examples include Robinia pseudoacacia, Pittosporum tobira and Lonicera japonica.
sub_hypo.relations: Introduction pathway differentiates growth form, stature and invaded niche breadth: unintentional introductions are associated with annual herbaceous growth, low stature and broad invaded niches, in contrast to predominantly perennial/woody gardening introductions. Pathway differences occur for growth form (p=3.2e-6), height (p=1.2e-5) and invaded niche breadth (p=0.047).

sub_hypo.text: New progressive urban or cropland expansion does not yet host the unintentional invasion assemblage associated with long-established urban landscapes.
sub_hypo.context: Sampled plots in Barcelona province, contrasting progressive landscape changes during 1956–2009 and 1993–2009 within 50 m with established urban landscapes.
sub_hypo.relations: Progressive expansion does not show the positive unintentional-invasion association characteristic of established urbanization; progressive change during 1956–2009 is negatively associated with unintentional counts (Spearman ρ=−0.13). Unintentional counts differ among trajectory groups (Kruskal-Wallis H=21.0, p=3e-5).

sub_hypo.text: Pathway-specific invasion types are phylogenetically structured, with adjacent tree tips sharing introduction pathways more often than expected by chance.
sub_hypo.context: Non-native plant species in the Barcelona province species dataset matched to the supplied phylogenetic tree; Opuntia ficus-indica entries are excluded from the phylogenetic analysis.
sub_hypo.relations: Introduction pathway clusters along the supplied Newick tree tip order: 55.1% of adjacent tips share a pathway versus 41.7% under the null expectation (p=0.008, 9999 permutations).

New progressive urban/cropland expansion does not (yet) host these unintentional invaders; the effect belongs to long-established urban landscapes. The pathway-specific invasion types are phylogenetically structured (adjacent tree tips share pathway more than expected by chance, p=0.008).
